name: Pacing / rhythm
controls: How time is spent: shot and scene durations, how much information arrives per second, how long things hold, where the beats fall, and how tension builds and releases.
question: How fast should the video move, and what sets its rhythm?
notes: Pacing is built from seven levers. Shot duration: average time between cuts or scene changes (ASL, average shot length). Information density: how many new things (words, elements, ideas) arrive per second; a rough ceiling for legible on-screen text is 3-4 words per second, and a new idea every 2-4 s for explanatory work. Breathing room: holds and negative time after a reveal so it registers; a reveal without a hold is lost. Rhythmic repetition: repeating the same durations or transition patterns so the viewer anticipates the next beat. Visual beats: moments of emphasis (a cut, an impact, a type slam) placed at regular or musical intervals. Anticipation: the wind-up before a beat (a pause, a squash, a riser, a slow-in) that makes it land. Payoff: the moment tension resolves, usually given the longest hold of the piece. Terms such as 'luxurious', 'snappy' and 'staccato' are informal practitioner language, not standardized; the prompts pin each to concrete numbers. Several options describe what drives timing (beat-, voiceover-, event-driven) rather than speed; pick the one that matters most and mention speed in the direction notes. Numbers assume 30 fps delivery.

options.what: Long shots, long holds, few elements per scene; time to look.
options.looks: Sparse compositions, one idea per shot, generous negative space.
options.motion: Long durations (800-1500 ms moves), gentle easing, slow camera drift.
options.use: Brand films, premium products, emotional or reflective pieces.
options.vs: Luxurious is slow plus polish and restraint signaling expense; meditative is slow with repetition and no narrative push.
options.prompt: Shots 4-8 s; element moves 800-1500 ms with smooth ease-in-out; holds >= 2 s after every reveal; at most one new element or line per 3 s; no cut shorter than 3 s.

options.what: Slow, controlled, deliberate timing that signals expense through restraint.
options.looks: Minimal elements, precise type, dark or neutral grounds, hero objects lit carefully.
options.motion: Very smooth long moves, slow reveals (masks, light sweeps), no bounces, perfect settles.
options.use: Luxury goods, flagship hardware, premium tiers, fashion.
options.vs: Slow can be plain or casual; luxurious is slow with precision and restraint. Cinematic may be fast in places; luxurious stays controlled.
options.prompt: Shots 4-7 s; moves 1000-2000 ms with long ease-out (expo or quart out) and no overshoot; light sweeps and mask reveals over 1.2-2 s; holds >= 2.5 s; max one word group on screen at a time; silence or near-silence between beats.

options.what: Very slow, repetitive, continuous motion with no push toward a climax.
options.looks: Soft forms, gradients, nature or abstract loops, almost no text.
options.motion: Cyclical motion with long periods (4-10 s), breathing scale, drifting particles.
options.vs: Slow still has narrative progression; meditative deliberately removes it. Loop-oriented pacing is about seamlessness, not mood.
options.prompt: No cuts, or crossfades of >= 2 s only; cyclical motion with periods of 4-10 s (e.g. a 4 s inhale / 6 s exhale scale of 1.00-1.08); no text or one line held >= 5 s; nothing moves faster than 5% of frame width per second.

options.what: Steady, readable pacing tuned so viewers can follow and understand each point.
options.looks: One idea per scene, labels and captions readable, diagrams building piece by piece.
options.motion: Moves 400-700 ms, consistent transitions, short holds after each point.
options.use: Explainers, tutorials, product demos, educational content.
options.vs: Voiceover-synchronized pacing is driven by the VO track; medium explanatory is a speed target that often (but not always) coincides.
options.prompt: Scenes 3-6 s; one new idea every 3-5 s; element moves 400-700 ms with ease-out; hold each completed state >= 1.2 s; on-screen text <= 3 words per second of hold time.

options.what: Quick cuts and brisk motion that keep energy high while staying readable.
options.looks: Bold, simple frames, large type, fewer words per card.
options.motion: Moves 200-400 ms, strong ease-outs, cuts every 1-2 s.
options.use: Launch trailers, social ads, sports, event openers.
options.vs: Hyper-fast pushes past comfortable readability; rapid-fire is fast with a flood of discrete items.
options.prompt: Shots 1-2 s; moves 200-400 ms with strong ease-out (power3/expo out); holds 0.6-1 s; <= 5 words per card; one visual change at least every 1.5 s.

options.what: Extremely rapid cutting and motion that deliberately overwhelms, used in bursts.
options.looks: Flash frames, single words, strobing color changes, dense collages.
options.motion: Cuts of 2-8 frames, instant transitions, very short moves (80-200 ms).
options.use: Trailer climaxes, hype reels, music videos, social hooks.
options.vs: Fast stays readable; hyper-fast trades readability for sensation. Use in bursts of 2-5 s, not whole pieces.
options.prompt: Burst sections of 2-5 s with cuts every 2-8 frames (70-270 ms at 30 fps), single words or single images per cut, instant or 80-150 ms transitions. Always follow a burst with a hold of >= 1.5 s so the key message lands. Avoid flashing faster than 3 times per second over large bright areas (photosensitivity).

options.what: Short, decisive motions that start fast and stop dead, with tight gaps between them.
options.looks: Clean UI and type that snaps into position.
options.motion: 150-350 ms moves, very strong ease-out (expo out), no lingering; small stagger (30-60 ms).
options.use: UI motion, product demos, SaaS launch films, social.
options.vs: Fast is about cut rate; snappy is about each motion's curve (quick, decisive settle). Staccato adds deliberate gaps of stillness between hits.
options.prompt: Every element move 150-350 ms with expo.out or power4.out, settling without overshoot; staggers 30-60 ms; scenes 1.5-3 s; holds 0.8-1.2 s. Nothing drifts: things arrive and stop.

options.what: Discrete hits separated by moments of stillness, like short detached musical notes.
options.looks: Elements appear in abrupt steps; frames alternate motion and stillness.
options.motion: Instant or near-instant appearances (0-150 ms), hard stops, holds of 300-800 ms between hits.
options.use: Typographic pieces, ads, music-driven edits, glitch or editorial styles.
options.vs: Snappy motions still travel smoothly; staccato removes the travel and emphasizes the stop. Continuous is its opposite.
options.prompt: Each beat is a hit: elements appear or jump position in 0-150 ms, then everything freezes for 300-800 ms before the next hit. Keep the hold length consistent (or tied to the tempo) so the rhythm reads. No continuous drift during holds.

options.what: No cuts: the piece plays as a single unbroken camera move or transformation.
options.looks: A connected world or canvas where every scene is reached by moving through space.
options.motion: Camera travels, zooms through objects, morphs; never a hard cut.
options.use: Product tours, infinite-canvas explainers, brand films, hero animations.
options.conveys: Coherence and immersion; everything is connected.
options.vs: Flowing describes the smoothness of motion; continuous is a structural rule: no cuts at all. Oner is film jargon for a single take.
options.prompt: Use zero hard cuts. Link every scene with a camera move, zoom-through or morph (600-1200 ms). Keep something in motion at all times, but slow the camera to near-stop for 1.5-2.5 s at each key point so information can be read.

options.what: Overlapping, smooth motion where one action leads into the next without hard stops.
options.looks: Soft shapes, curves, gradients; elements pass the baton to each other.
options.motion: Overlapping action, long ease-in-outs, motion paths on curves, moves that start before previous ones end.
options.use: Brand films, wellness, consumer apps, abstract pieces.
options.vs: Continuous forbids cuts; flowing can include cuts but motion is always smooth and overlapping. Snappy is its opposite.
options.prompt: Overlap every action: the next move starts at 50-70% of the previous one. Moves 600-1200 ms with sine or power2 in-out; curved motion paths; no hard stops (every element eases to rest). Transitions are dissolves, morphs or match moves, never hard cuts.

options.what: Visual events land on a steady pulse (a tempo grid), whether or not specific music is locked.
options.looks: Repeating visual units, cuts and hits at regular intervals.
options.motion: Cuts and key poses on beats (e.g. every 500 ms at 120 BPM); secondary motion on half beats.
options.use: Promos, social ads, montages, typography pieces.
options.conveys: Energy and groove; the piece feels 'tight'.
options.vs: Music-synchronized locks to a specific track's structure (drops, phrases); beat-driven only needs a consistent tempo grid.
search: cut to the beat motion graphics
options.prompt: Pick a tempo (e.g. 120 BPM = 500 ms per beat) and place every cut and key pose on a beat; changes of scene on bar lines (every 4 beats = 2 s). Secondary motion on half beats. Keep entrances short enough (<= 1 beat) that each hit lands on the grid.

options.what: Timing follows a specific track: phrases, builds, drops and accents drive scene changes and emphasis.
options.looks: Scene structure mirrors song structure; big visual moments on drops.
options.motion: Cuts on downbeats, hits on accents, energy tracking the arrangement, stillness on breakdowns.
options.use: Trailers, launch films, recaps, music visualizers.
options.vs: Beat-driven follows a generic pulse; music-synchronized follows the actual track's sections and accents.
options.prompt: Map the track first: intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro, with timestamps. Change scenes on phrase boundaries (every 4 or 8 bars), put the hero reveal exactly on the drop, cut on downbeats during high energy, and slow to long holds during breakdowns.

options.what: The narration track sets timing: visuals change with sentences and key words appear as they're spoken.
options.looks: Visuals and on-screen words illustrating exactly what's being said.
options.motion: Scene changes at sentence ends, emphasis animations on stressed words, holds during pauses.
options.vs: Medium explanatory is a speed; VO-synchronized is a timing source (the VO could be fast or slow). Word sync in the sound dimension is the finer-grained technique.
options.prompt: Time scene changes to sentence boundaries (cut 100-200 ms after the last word). Make on-screen keywords appear within +/- 3 frames of being spoken. Hold visuals through VO pauses; never show a visual that contradicts or precedes its line by more than 0.5 s.

options.what: Timing is set by in-world actions: a click, a data update, a trigger causing a reaction.
options.looks: UI or systems responding to triggers; cursor actions, notifications, state changes.
options.motion: Idle, then action, then immediate reaction and cascade; waits between events are natural, not metered.
options.use: Product demos, UI walkthroughs, simulations, workflow demos.
options.vs: Beat-driven follows a clock; event-driven follows causes. Informal term.
options.prompt: Every change is triggered by a visible event (click, keystroke, message arriving). Reaction starts within 50-100 ms of the trigger; cascades stagger 60-120 ms; between events, hold 0.8-1.5 s in a readable idle state with subtle life (cursor drift, live indicator).

options.what: Deliberate stillness and silence are used as structural elements to create weight.
options.looks: Frames that hold still; empty frames; single words alone.
options.motion: Motion bursts separated by long pauses of 1-3 s; silence before key reveals.
options.use: Manifestos, teasers, premium launches, dramatic statements.
options.vs: Staccato pauses are short and rhythmic; pause-heavy pauses are long and dramatic.
options.prompt: Follow each key reveal with 1.5-3 s of complete stillness. Before the biggest reveal, cut to an empty frame or a near-still for 0.8-1.5 s. Motion itself can be quick (300-500 ms); the stillness carries the weight.

options.what: A sequence of short shots cut together to compress time or convey breadth and feeling.
options.looks: Many different images or scenes, unified by grade, type or transition.
options.motion: Cuts every 0.5-2 s, often to music, with building rhythm.
options.use: Recaps, trailers, brand films, feature sizzles.
options.vs: Rapid-fire is a flood of discrete informational items; montage is associative imagery building a feeling.
options.prompt: Cut 8-20 shots at 0.5-2 s each, unified by one grade and one transition style. Group shots into 2-3 phrases that accelerate (2 s -> 1 s -> 0.5 s) and end each phrase with a longer hold (2 s).

options.what: A quick succession of discrete items (features, stats, words, logos) delivered one after another.
options.looks: Same template repeated with swapping content; counters or lists.
options.motion: Items swap every 300-800 ms with identical transitions, sometimes accelerating.
options.use: Feature lists, integration logos, changelogs, social hooks.
options.vs: Montage is associative imagery; rapid-fire is a list. Hyper-fast is about raw cut speed regardless of content.
options.prompt: Present 8-20 items in one fixed template, swapping every 300-800 ms with identical transitions (e.g. 120 ms vertical flip). Optionally accelerate across the sequence; end with a hold of >= 1.5 s on a summary line ('and 200+ more').

options.what: Timing designed around a seamless repeat: evenly distributed events and a matched start/end.
options.looks: Self-contained cycle; no intro or outro.
options.motion: Events spaced evenly across the loop duration; all properties return to initial values.
options.use: Hero loops, social loops, backgrounds, GIFs.
options.vs: Meditative is a mood; loop-oriented is a structural timing constraint that can be fast or slow.
options.prompt: Choose a loop length (4-12 s) and distribute events evenly across it so there is no lull at the seam. All animated properties must return to their starting values at the last frame; the first 0.5 s and last 0.5 s must match in speed so the join is invisible.
